title: Rhythm and blues sessions versus Bechet and Jelly Roll dates
summary: Asked whether 1950s r&b work felt like baby music, Bunn says he did his best and was simply paid for it.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Well, looking at your career, like, in the --
No. I was just thinking about what you did in the late '40s, '50s and into the '60s, it seemed like the actual jazz people -- the younger jazz players, were moving more into the bebop and --
Yeah. So you did a lot more recordings in the rhythm and blues and --
And so forth. How did you feel about that music? I mean in some ways it was simpler music.
I didn't pay it no mind.
It'd just come up in a session and I knew they'd
paid for it, I just done it.
But when I listen to -- I was listening the other night to your recordings that you did with Sidney Bechet and with Jelly Roll and a couple of those.
And the playing there is -- the music is asking a lot more of you. You've got to be on your toes, you know.
So I felt like some of your best playing was in those kinds of things, whereas like --
And anyway I tried to go up to do anything I knew I had a record date.
Understand? I did my best. Every one I went on I did my best.

I know you did because that's the kind of person you are. But that's not the question I'm asking. I'm asking did you feel after awhile that some of the music you were playing in the '50s was kind of baby music, or that it was boring?
I didn't pay no mind. I knew I was getting paid for it so I had to do it, I done it.
And I think that's the right feeling.
